title: BRICS Summit 2026: India's Global South Outreach Courted ASEAN, Africa, GCC and BIMSTEC
excerpt: At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India used its presidency to bring the chairs of ASEAN, the African Union, CELAC, the GCC and BIMSTEC into the conversation on the Global South — closing with the unanimous New Delhi Declaration.
body:
• India used its 2026 BRICS presidency to hold outreach sessions with the country chairs of ASEAN, the African Union, CELAC, the Gulf Cooperation Council and BIMSTEC during the September 12-13 summit in New Delhi.
  • MEA secretary (Economic Relations) Sudhakar Dalela said the two days of discussion centred on how BRICS can deliver "outcomes and initiatives relevant to the Global South."
  • PM Modi, chairing the plenary session, said trust in BRICS has grown because Global South voices are heard — and warned that unequal access to strategic technologies could hold back developing economies.
  • The 18th summit closed with the unanimous adoption of the 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration; South Africa's president confirmed China will host the next summit in 2027.

The outreach sessions

India used its BRICS presidency to widen the summit's table. Alongside the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, Indian officials held outreach sessions with the country chairs of developing-country groupings from other regions — ASEAN, the African Union, CELAC for Latin America and the Caribbean, the Gulf Cooperation Council and BIMSTEC.

"It was felt that perhaps it would be a good idea to reach out to other continents," MEA secretary (Economic Relations) Sudhakar Dalela said, according to ANI. The invited countries were chosen to ensure representation of the most important developing regions, and to share the group's work with its partners in the Global South.

"I can say from personal experience that the trust of Global South nations in BRICS has grown, because their voices are heard, their experiences are respected, and solutions are crafted not just for them, but with them."

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

Context & Background

The outreach continues a theme from India's 2023 G20 presidency — positioning India as a bridge between the Global South and the major powers. Its 2026 BRICS chairship involved more than 400 meetings and engagements across 30 Indian cities, according to the declaration text.

The backdrop was tense. BRICS foreign ministers failed to issue a joint statement at their May meeting in New Delhi, and US President Donald Trump had threatened members with tariffs of up to 10 percent over the bloc's "anti-American" policies, per Forbes India. Against that history, the declaration's unanimous adoption — Modi announced that "no member has raised any objection" — was itself a signal of cohesion.

The 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration covered familiar BRICS territory: UN Security Council and Bretton Woods reform, cross-border payment interoperability and local-currency trade settlement, AI governance, WTO dispute-settlement reform, energy security, and a condemnation of the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack "in the strongest terms." It registered "deep concern" over escalating West Asia tensions without naming any country.

Impact & Analysis

The outreach sessions produced no communique of their own, but they served a strategic purpose: demonstrating that BRICS is not a closed club. With members accounting for roughly half of the world's population, 40 percent of global GDP and 26 percent of global trade, per Forbes India, the bloc's claim to speak for the developing world carries weight — and inviting regional groupings to watch it in action reinforces that claim.

Still, the declaration's silences were telling. The Russia-Ukraine war went unnamed anywhere in the text, and leaders acknowledged there is "no one-size-fits-all approach" on de-dollarisation — signs that consensus among members with divergent interests has real limits.

"We adhere to a multilateral system where there is no dominance of one player or country over others; where we want countries in BRICS, and indeed countries outside of BRICS as well, to respect one another."

— Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa

Diaspora Angle

For India's diaspora, the choice of outreach partners matters directly. The GCC hosts one of the largest concentrations of Indian expatriates anywhere, and the summit's agenda — energy security, payment-system interoperability, local-currency trade settlement and a logistics cooperation framework — touches the livelihoods of Indian workers and businesses across the Gulf. Lower remittance costs and smoother trade flows are the kind of concrete gains they stand to feel.

The engagement with ASEAN, BIMSTEC and the African Union likewise connects to established Indian business and trading communities in Southeast Asia and East and Southern Africa — economies that millions of overseas Indians call home.

What's Next

The chairship now rotates to China, which will host the 19th BRICS Summit in 2027 — confirmed by Ramaphosa at the closing briefing, according to South Africa's official news service. Whether the declaration's commitments on payment interoperability, quota reform and counter-terrorism translate into institutional action will be closely watched. India exits its presidency having kept the bloc united through a difficult year and visibly widened its conversation with the Global South.
